summary: Describes the role of link indications, information from the link layer to higher layers about link state, in the Internet architecture. Used well, they can improve performance, but misuse can hurt robustness and performance. The memo summarizes proposals and architectural issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The cable layer can tell the layers above, hey, I just lost the signal. This note asks when listening is smart and when it causes trouble.

questions: how should higher layers use link layer information
what are the security risks of link indications
subtitle: How the link layer can safely tell higher layers about connection quality

tldr.problem: The link layer (the layer connecting hardware) knows useful information about connection quality that higher-layer protocols could use to optimize performance. However, passing this information up the stack must be done carefully to avoid breaking reliability.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes a layered indication model where the link layer sends abstract signals about link state (up/down) and quality (rate, loss, delay) to the Internet and transport layers, which validate and filter them before acting on them.
tldr.outcome: Properly architected link indications can improve performance in routing and congestion control, but protocols that use them must account for real-world link behavior: asymmetry, flapping between up and down states, and unreliable signal strength measurements.

today: RFC 4907 is an informational memo from the Internet Architecture Board. It is not an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted. The principles it outlines remain relevant to the design of protocols that use link-layer information, especially in wireless and mobile networks.

sections.title: Link Indications in the Internet Architecture
sections.content:
Link indications are messages from the link layer—the hardware level—to higher-layer software, reporting the state of the connection. The simplest examples are 'Link Up' (the connection works) and 'Link Down' (the connection is broken).

The Internet architecture carefully separates concerns: the link layer shields higher layers from hardware details, but sometimes it has useful information that could help performance. Under ideal conditions, a link is either reliably working or completely down. Real-world links are messier: wireless links may flap between states, wired links may fail in one direction only, and signals degrade unpredictably. This memo outlines when link indications help and when they cause problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of your computer's network stack can ask the cable 'are you working?'. This RFC explains how to ask and when to trust the answer.

sections.title: How Indications Flow Through the Layers
sections.content:
The layered indication model shows how information moves between the link layer and higher layers without each layer needing to know about hardware details.

The Internet layer validates and filters link indications, deciding which ones matter for routing and IP configuration. After a 'Link Up' signal, the host checks that the IP address configuration is still valid. The transport layer uses indications for parameter estimation—adjusting how aggressively it sends data based on signals about loss and delay. However, the transport layer does not tear down connections on 'Link Down' events alone, since these may be temporary.

Applications should not read link indications directly. A 'Link Up' event means hardware is working, not that the network is configured. Applications should respond to transport layer signals instead, which have more reliable meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Different layers handle different news from the cable. The lowest layer says 'signal quality changed'. The middle layer thinks 'maybe the route needs updating'. The top layer (your app) only cares when the whole connection dies.

sections.title: Key Architectural Principles
sections.content:
Using link indications safely requires several principles. First, proposals must validate that their assumptions about link behavior hold in practice. Simple models—where a link is either reliably up or completely down—fail in real wireless networks, where links exhibit asymmetry (working better in one direction), intermittent loss, and rapid state changes.

Second, link indications must be clearly defined: 'Link Down' might mean 'no frames transmitted successfully in the last second' or 'received an explicit disconnect frame', with different implications for what has actually failed.

Third, protocols using indications must stay robust if indications are wrong. The Internet was designed to recover from transient errors without explicit notification. Assuming link indications are accurate can break this robustness. Upper layers should validate indications and limit the damage from false ones.

Fourth, proposals must maintain effective congestion control: if link indications cause the transport layer to send faster, but the bottleneck is actually congestion further down the path, loss will increase. Finally, proposals must not require link indications for basic interoperability: networks should keep working even if one end ignores indications.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are: test your assumptions, define clearly what signals mean, don't break if a signal is wrong, don't accidentally cause congestion, and always have a backup plan without the signals.

sections.title: Avoiding Race Conditions and Instability
sections.content:
Complexity arises when multiple layers of the stack respond to link indications simultaneously. If routing decides to switch to a different interface while the transport layer is re-estimating its parameters for the old path, the two may disagree about what the network looks like, leading to poor performance decisions.

When the Internet layer detects a path change—a major change in transmission rate or a switch to a different interface—it should reset transport parameters to their initial values, allowing them to be re-estimated on the new path. Relying on layering helps too: applications should not read link indications directly, but trust the Internet and transport layers to filter out transient events.

Metrics used for routing and for link enablement decisions should be consistent. If routing chooses a link based on one quality measure (e.g., expected transmission count) but the handoff decision uses another (e.g., signal strength), the system may oscillate, repeatedly switching between interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: When the cable sends multiple signals at once, different parts of the computer might make conflicting decisions. The fix is to reset estimates when something big changes, let each layer filter for the one below, and use the same measurements everywhere.

sections.title: Security and Spoofing Risks
sections.content:
Link layer control frames are often unprotected, allowing attackers to forge them. For example, WiFi management frames (associate, disassociate, deauthenticate) can be spoofed. An attacker forging 'Link Down' indications could cause denial of service.

Even where the link layer incorporates security, inconsistencies can create problems. WiFi with encryption (802.11i) requires an authenticated key exchange before any data can be sent, meaning 'Link Up' should not be declared until that exchange completes. However, the standard does not protect management frames, so an attacker can still send a spoofed deauthenticate frame to disconnect stations.

The transport and application layers must validate link indications before taking action. For example, receiving an isolated ICMP error message does not necessarily mean a connection is broken—the error may be transient. Robust protocols wait for repeated failures or explicit signals from the routing layer before assuming a connection is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can forge the cable's messages. Even with encryption, there are gaps. So the upper layers should verify that a bad signal is real before actually giving up.
